AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: Non-invasive evaluation of muscle perfusion using near infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) coupled with a vascular occlusion test (VOT) may provide an early and simple marker of altered perfusion and microcirculatory function in sepsis.

AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: To compare the time-course of NIRS-derived variables with systemic measures of perfusion in an experimental model of peritonitis.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: Peritonitis was induced in eight anesthetized, mechanically ventilated, adult sheep (24-34 Kg), by injecting autologous feces into the peritoneal cavity. Animals were followed until death or for a maximum of 30 hours. Muscle tissue oxygen saturation (StO2) was determined using NIRS on the right posterior leg and arterial VOTs were performed by intermittent intra-aortic balloon inflation. Microdialysis was used to measure muscle lactate and pyruvate levels.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Muscle StO2 was significantly lower than baseline values from 8 hours after sepsis induction, but with considerable inter-subject variability. The NIRS VOT ascending (Asc) slope decreased to values <120%/min in most animals from 12 hours after sepsis induction. Muscle lactate/pyruvate ratios were higher than baseline from 16 hours after sepsis induction. Mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) decreased to <70% and blood lactate levels increased to >2 mmol/L in most of the animals only 24 and 28 hours after sepsis induction, respectively. Muscle NIRS StO2 correlated strongly with femoral venous oxygen saturation (r = 0.820) and moderately with SvO2 (r = 0.436).

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: The muscle NIRS Asc Slope after a VOT is altered earlier than global markers of tissue hypoperfusion during sepsis. This simple non-invasive test can detect early changes in peripheral perfusion in sepsis.

Article.ArticleTitle: Peripheral Muscle Near-Infrared Spectroscopy (NIRS) Variables are Altered Early in Septic Shock.
